    Picking a base model

    After this lesson you can name the dimensions a base-model choice trades against — license, tokenizer, instruct quality, context length, size, community — and pick a sensible starting point for a project (or explain why this Academy defaults to SmolLM2-135M-Instruct).

    Level: beginner Read time: ~9 min Prerequisites: Base vs instruct models Updated: 13 Nov 2026

    There is no universal "best" SLM. There are constraints, and the smallest model that meets your constraints is the right one to start with. The previous lesson sorted out which flavour of a family to use (usually: instruct). This lesson is the checklist for picking which family in the first place.

    The dimensions that matter

    A base-model choice is a trade across six dimensions. Walk down the list, write the constraints your project actually has, and the field of candidates narrows fast:

    • License — can you legally ship what you train from it?
    • Tokenizer family — a contract with your dataset and a hard constraint for distillation.
    • Instruct quality — how aligned is the starting point already?
    • Context length — how long is your input plus output?
    • Size & latency budget — what fits, what's fast enough, what costs what?
    • Community — does the ecosystem, including your serving stack, support what you want to do next?

    License: can you ship this commercially?

    Check the license before training, not at deploy. Permissive licences (Apache 2.0, MIT) let you fine-tune and ship a commercial product without much friction. Others — research-only, non-commercial, "acceptable use" addenda — restrict what you can do with derivatives. Several popular open families use a custom community licence with its own conditions, such as a user-count threshold or an acceptable-use policy, so read it rather than assume. A fine-tune doesn't reset the licence; the parent model's terms travel with it.

    Data carries terms too. The datasets you fine-tune on have licences, and text generated by another model can come with that model's terms of use. Record where every training row came from, so you can answer the question when someone asks.

    For this Academy we use a permissively licensed family (Apache 2.0) so every reader can take what they learn into a product without a legal review.

    Tokenizer: a contract with your data

    The tokenizer is the rule that turns text into the model's vocabulary (Lesson 0.4). A few practical reasons it matters when you pick:

    • Vocab efficiency on your data. Different tokenizers split your domain differently. Code-heavy data tokenizes more efficiently under a tokenizer trained on code; multilingual data needs a multilingual tokenizer to avoid blowing up sequence lengths.
    • Special-token expectations. Instruct models bake their chat template into specific special tokens — they aren't interchangeable across families.
    • A hard constraint for logit distillation. Logit-level knowledge distillation (Track 4, Lesson 4.2) trains the student to match the teacher's probabilities over specific tokens. If teacher and student don't share a tokenizer, the two vocabularies don't line up token for token, so those targets have to be mapped across (some tokens won't map) or matched with a cross-tokenizer method such as Universal Logit Distillation. Sequence-level distillation, training the student on the teacher's generated text, works across tokenizers. Picking teacher and student from the same family keeps every option open.

    Instruct quality: how aligned is the starting point?

    Not all instruct models are equally well-tuned. Some refuse confidently; some are chatty; some hold formats well; some drift. The cheapest way to find out is to load two or three candidate instruct models, hand them a few of your real prompts, and look at the raw outputs. Baseline quality is your starting line. A fine-tune lifts it, but starting closer to the answer means cheaper, faster lifts.

    Then make it a number: score each candidate, untouched, on your held-out examples. That baseline is what any fine-tune has to beat. BrewSLM records it for you: after each real training run it scores the base model on the same held-out split and reports the lift (Lesson 0.9 explains why this comes first).

    Context length: how long is your input?

    Modern SLMs ship with context windows from 2k to 256k tokens and beyond. Match this to your task's actual input length distribution, not the worst case from a paper. A model's maximum context costs nothing until you use it: attention compute and KV-cache memory scale with the tokens you actually send. Long-context capability matters only if your inputs need it, and quality at long context is often worse than the headline number, so check it on your data.

    Size & latency budget: small first, step up with reason

    Default to the smallest model that plausibly works for the task. Common starting points: 135M, 360M, 1B, 1.5B, 3B. Step up to 7B only when the smaller model demonstrably can't clear your gold-set bar after honest data work — not because bigger sounds safer.

    The cost is not just GPU memory at training (Track 1, Lesson 1.15). A 7B model needs about 7× the memory and roughly 7× the per-token compute of a 1B model at inference too (and about 50× a 135M model), every request, forever. If a 1B model gets you to your quality gate, ship the 1B.

    "Small first" can fail — be honest about it

    If your task genuinely requires broad world knowledge or multi-step reasoning, no amount of LoRA on a 135M model will get you there. That's the lesson of LLMs vs SLMs made concrete: small models give some things up. If your eval makes that clear, stepping up to a larger model — or switching to RAG, or distilling from a bigger teacher — is the right answer, not more epochs.

    Community: who else is fine-tuning on this?

    A model with an active fine-tuning community is a model you can ride: more recipes, more reported quirks, more shared evals, more tools that work on day one. Hugging Face download counts, the number of public LoRA adapters in the family, the activity on the model card's issues — all rough but useful signals. Picking an obscure model is fine if you have a strong reason; otherwise the safe pick is one the ecosystem already knows.

    Check the serving side too. A brand-new architecture, such as a hybrid that mixes attention with linear-attention layers (Lesson 0.7), can train fine in Transformers but not yet convert to GGUF for llama.cpp, or not yet run in your inference server. Support usually arrives, but sometimes weeks or months later. Before you commit, export and serve the untouched base model once in the runtime you plan to ship on.

    Why this Academy uses SmolLM2-135M-Instruct

    Concretely, the choice for the whole course is a trade matching the constraints above:

    • License: Apache 2.0 — you can ship a commercial fine-tune.
    • Tokenizer: HF-native, shared across the SmolLM2 family — leaves the door open for distillation across sizes.
    • Instruct quality: usable baseline alignment; well-behaved chat template.
    • Context length: 8k positions in the shipped config (max_position_embeddings: 8192); quality at long context is unmeasured for the 135M model, so keep inputs short. In practice the limit is the training run's own maximum sequence length (BrewSLM's default is 2,048 tokens), which is plenty for classification, extraction and short Q&A: the Academy's running tasks fit.
    • Size: 135M parameters — fits comfortably on a single consumer GPU, and runs inference fast enough on a CPU (training on a CPU is slow), so every reader can follow along without a server.
    • Community: HF-native, broad tooling support; vLLM, llama.cpp / GGUF, peft / TRL all work day one.

    Key idea

    There is no universal best — pick the smallest model that meets your licence, tokenizer, context, and quality constraints. The instinct to "just use the biggest" is exactly backwards: bigger means more memory, more latency, more cost on every request, forever. Step up only when the small model demonstrably can't.

    That ends the Foundations track. You now know what a model is, how it learns, how text becomes tokens, how attention and the Transformer work, how a language model predicts the next token, the four levers you can pull, the trade between large and small, what an instruct model is, and how to pick a base. Track 1 goes deep on supervised fine-tuning itself.

    Recap

    • Filter candidates by hard constraints first: model and data licence, tokenizer and language fit, context length, and serving-stack support.
    • Start with the smallest size that plausibly works and step up one rung only when a measured result says so.
    • Score each candidate's untouched baseline on your held-out set; that is the bar the fine-tune must beat.

    Try it (5 minutes)

    You are building a commercial email router for German and English mail. Inputs are up to 1,500 tokens. Four candidates: (A) 360M, Apache 2.0, English-only tokenizer, 8k context; (B) 1.5B, research-only licence, multilingual, 32k context; (C) 1B, Apache 2.0, multilingual tokenizer, 32k context; (D) 3B, Apache 2.0, multilingual, 32k context. Walk the flow: which candidates drop out, and which do you baseline first?

    Show answer

    B drops at the licence check: research-only rules out a commercial product. A is doubtful at the tokenizer check: an English-only tokenizer splits German into many more tokens and the model saw little German, so check its token counts and a few outputs on real German mail before keeping it. Context is fine for all of them (1,500 tokens plus a short label). So baseline C first, the smallest candidate that clearly passes, and keep D as the next rung if C plateaus below your bar after honest data work. If A's German outputs look usable, its baseline costs little to add.

    Key terms

    Model license
    The terms attached to a base model that travel with every derivative — including your fine-tune. Check before training, not at deploy.
    Tokenizer family
    A shared vocabulary and special-token set across a model family; needed for straightforward logit-level distillation and shared chat templates.
    Instruct quality
    How well an instruct model already follows instructions and respects formats before any fine-tuning; the starting line a fine-tune lifts from.
    Context length
    The maximum tokens the model can take in plus produce; pick to match your real input/output distribution, not the worst case.
    Small first
    Default to the smallest model that plausibly works; step up only when the eval makes the case.
    Baseline
    The untouched candidate's score on your held-out set; the bar the fine-tune must beat.
    Data licence
    The terms on your training data, including data generated by another model; they travel with the fine-tune too.
    Community support
    Active fine-tunes, shared evals, tools that work day one; the practical reason to favour well-known families when other constraints tie.
